stories.title: How Much Money Do MLM Participants Actually Make?
alternates: Can You Really Get Rich Recruiting People Into an MLM?
What MLM Income Disclosures Admit in the Fine Print
stories.question: How much money do MLM participants actually make?
stories.whyWatch: Everyone has been pitched by a friend. The companies' own income disclosures, a nationally representative survey and a 30-company analysis all say the same thing, and the pitch's central promise, leveraged income from a downline, is where the numbers are most revealing.
stories.tension: The pitch sells leverage: recruit and earn from everyone below you. The disclosures show the leverage is real for a fraction of a percent and the structure guarantees most people sit at the bottom.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Income distributions for participants net of expenses, and evidence on whether income comes from recruiting or retail sales.

FTC MLM income disclosure report 2024: right (0.5, direct)
Taylor, The Case against MLM: right (0.55, direct)

FTC MLM income disclosure report 2024: partly (0.3, direct)

stories.premise: Four independent documents answer the question the same way, each with a limit the video must state. AARP's 2018 probability sample of 601 participants found 47% lost money and 25% made any profit, self-reported. The FTC's 2024 review of 70 income disclosures found most participants made $1,000 or less a year, before expenses. Taylor's analysis of 30 companies gets to 99.6% losing money only after subtracting required purchases, so that figure depends on his method. The downline promise is structurally true (the pay plans do route income from recruits) and practically false for almost everyone: in rank tables over 90% sit in the lowest cohort averaging under $100. The exhaustion arithmetic is illustrated by Taylor, not tested by any study.

arc.hook: A friend's message: join under me, build a team, earn while you sleep. How much do people in that position actually make?
arc.conflict: The companies publish income disclosures. Read one aloud: median earnings, share with zero income, and what the fine print says is not deducted.
arc.evidence: AARP's survey (47% lost money), the FTC's 70-disclosure review (most under $1,000 a year before expenses), Taylor's 30-company analysis (99.6% lose after required purchases, by his method), and the rank tables showing where the downline income goes.
arc.resolution: The leverage exists, for the top fraction of a percent, because the plans pay for recruiting rather than retail; most participants are structurally at the bottom.
arc.takeaway: Ask for the income disclosure before joining, read the expense fine print, and treat 'leveraged income' as the company's revenue model rather than yours.

coherence.explanation: One question, how much MLM participants earn, answered in three acts: the income distribution, where the money comes from (recruiting, not retail), and why the structure keeps most people at the bottom. Wholesaling and rental-property debt were a different subject and are dropped.

stories.title: Do 97% of Day Traders Really Lose Money?
alternates: Can Anyone Make a Living Day Trading?
What Happens to People Who Day Trade for a Year
stories.question: Do most people who day trade lose money, and can anyone beat the odds?
stories.whyWatch: Sixteen sources in the corpus say most day traders lose, and the pitch videos say a disciplined strategy beats that. Two complete-market datasets, Brazil and Taiwan, let the viewer see the whole distribution, including the winners.
stories.tension: The pitch: discipline and a proven strategy make you consistently profitable. The data: a small minority is predictably profitable, and the longer people trade the smaller their chance of being in it.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Complete trading records for a population of day traders over at least a year, net of fees, with the share who profit and whether it rises with experience.

Taiwan day-trader study (Barber et al.): right (0.7, direct)
ESMA CFD intervention 2018: partly (0.5, partial)

Taiwan day-trader study (Barber et al.): partly (0.4, direct)
gaps: No study strong enough to decide: "Trading fewer, higher-quality setups beats frequent trading because fees and fatigue erode returns"
stories.premise: The Brazilian study followed 1,551 people who day traded index futures for more than 300 days: 97% lost money net of fees, and the share with a positive result fell with every extra day traded. The Taiwan study covers every day trader on the exchange from 1992 to 2006 and finds reliably negative returns before and after costs. Both find a small, predictably profitable minority (under 3%), which is the honest form of the 'disciplined strategy' claim. Limits the video must carry: Brazil is index futures and Taiwan is stocks in an earlier era; the HFT finding is from futures; the EU CFD figures are a different product; and nothing here measures momentum-stock traders, so the claim that an expert can multiply an account in a month is unchecked rather than refuted.

arc.hook: A screenshot of a small account turned into a large one in a month. How often does that happen to people who try?
arc.conflict: The sources promise consistency with discipline; the regulators and academics who can see every account say most lose.
arc.evidence: Brazil: 1,551 persistent traders, 97% lost, the best averaged US$310 a day with a standard deviation of US$2,560. Taiwan: every trader on the exchange, losses before and after costs in every year but one. Both: a predictably profitable minority under 3%, and no learning curve.
arc.resolution: Day trading is possible to win at and overwhelmingly lost at; frequency and fees erode results, and retail traders face algorithms with a structural edge. The evidence does not touch the exceptional-month story, so say so.
arc.takeaway: Treat day trading as an expensive hobby with a small chance of being in the 3%, and treat any strategy sold as consistent as a claim its seller must prove with audited records.

coherence.explanation: One question, whether most people who day trade lose and whether anyone beats the odds, answered by the base rate, the size of the profitable minority, the HFT explanation and the effect of trading frequency. Options strategies and sports betting are different markets with their own evidence and are dropped.

stories.title: Is 'Commission-Free' Trading Actually Free?
alternates: Who Pays When Your Broker Charges Nothing?
The Hidden Cost Inside Zero-Commission Trades
stories.question: Is commission-free trading actually free?
stories.whyWatch: Most retail traders use a zero-commission app. The paper on retail options trading puts a number on what they pay instead, and it is larger than the commissions were.
stories.tension: 'Free' on the screen; a 12.3% average quoted spread on the weekly options retail prefers, paid for by order flow.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Measured payment for order flow and effective spreads paid by retail, and evidence on whether removing commissions changed how much people trade.
evidenceAvailable: Retail options study (Bryzgalova et al.): right (0.65, direct)
Retail options study (Bryzgalova et al.): right (0.7, direct)
Retail options study (Bryzgalova et al.): right (0.5, direct)
Brazil day-trader study (Chague et al.): right (0.4, direct)
eToro crypto retail study (Kogan et al.): wrong (0.25, partial)
stories.premise: Bryzgalova and colleagues document that zero-commission brokers are paid for order flow by wholesalers and that the true cost sits in spreads: 17.2% average quoted spread on S&P 500 stock options against 3.55 basis points on the stocks, 12.3% on the sub-week options retail favours, with indirect spread costs of $4.13bn dwarfing $0.8bn of commissions. The boom is descriptive, not causal: the same paper and the Brazilian study link zero commissions to a surge in retail and day trading, while an eToro test found no change in one measure of trading intensity after commissions were removed. The video should present that as a limit on the boom claim, not on the cost claim.

arc.hook: Your trade cost nothing. Someone paid your broker for it. What did you pay?
arc.conflict: Free trading was sold as democratising markets; the paper says the cost moved rather than vanished, and moved most for the products retail likes best.
arc.evidence: Payment for order flow, quoted spreads on options versus stocks, the dollar totals, and the post-2019 surge in retail and options volume, with the eToro null result as the caveat.
arc.resolution: Free is a pricing model: commissions became spreads and order-flow payments, heaviest on short-dated options.
arc.takeaway: Count the spread, not the commission, and be most careful with the products the app makes easiest to trade.

coherence.explanation: One question, whether zero-commission trading is free, answered by who pays the broker (order flow), where the cost reappears (spreads, especially on options) and what free trading did to trading volume.
